1.translation: By the division of renunciation and relinquishment, he clearly states in the eighteenth chapter, in the determination of the highest truth, a summary of the meaning of the entire Gītā. Here, in passages such as ‘having mentally renounced all actions, the self-controlled one sits happily’ and ‘whose self is joined to the yoga of renunciation,’ renunciation of action has been taught. Likewise, in passages such as ‘having abandoned attachment to the fruit of action, ever content, without dependence’ and ‘therefore perform the relinquishment of all fruits of action, self-controlled,’ performance of action with relinquishment of the fruit alone has been taught. And the omniscient, supremely compassionate Lord would not teach things mutually contradictory. Therefore Arjuna, wishing to know the manner in which renunciation of action and its performance are not contradictory, said, ‘of renunciation.’ O Hṛṣīkeśa, controller of all the senses; O slayer of Keśin. Keśin was the great horse-shaped demon who, in battle, came with mouth opened to devour; into his mouth, opened exceedingly wide, He inserted His left arm, and at that very moment, with that same arm grown immense, split him like a cucumber and slew him. Hence the address ‘O mighty-armed one.’ I wish to know, by separate discrimination, the truth of renunciation and of relinquishment.

2.translation: To this the Blessed Lord gives the answer with ‘of desire-motivated actions.’ Actions enjoined with a condition of desire, such as ‘one desiring a son should sacrifice’ and ‘one desiring heaven should sacrifice,’ are desire-motivated actions. The poets know the laying down, the abandonment, of those actions as renunciation. The learned know the laying down of all actions together with their proper fruits as renunciation: this is the meaning. The skilled, discerning ones call relinquishment the relinquishment only of the fruits of all desire-motivated, obligatory, and occasional actions, not abandonment of action in its own form. Objection: because no fruit is heard for obligatory and occasional actions, how could there be relinquishment of a fruit that does not exist? There cannot be abandonment of a barren woman’s son. Answer: although in statements such as ‘one should worship at the junctions of day every day’ and ‘one should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives,’ no particular fruit is heard, as it is in ‘one desiring heaven’ or ‘one desiring cattle,’ nevertheless an injunction, being unable to set a discerning person in motion toward an activity that serves no human end, necessarily implies some fruit in general, just as in ‘one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit.’ Nor should it be thought, through excessive reverence for the teacher’s view, that the accomplishment of the injunction itself is the purpose of the injunction, because the impossibility of human activity without a purpose is difficult to avoid. A fruit is also heard even for obligatory rites, in passages such as ‘all these become inhabitants of meritorious worlds,’ ‘by action, the world of the fathers,’ and ‘by dharma he drives away sin.’ Therefore it is rightly said, ‘the discerning call relinquishment the relinquishment of all fruits of action.’ Objection: with relinquishment of fruit, would there not again be non-performance of fruitless actions? No; because all actions are assigned, through conjunction and separateness, for the purpose of the desire to know. Thus the Śruti says, ‘Brāhmaṇas desire to know this Self through recitation of the Veda, sacrifice, gift, and austerity consisting in not destroying.’ Therefore, abandoning as binding every fruit stated in each separate passage, performance of all actions for the purpose of the desire to know is entirely coherent. The desire to know is the inward inclination of the intellect, through discrimination between the eternal and non-eternal and through cessation of identification with the body. Until that point, for purification of sattva, while performing appropriate necessary action that does not conflict with knowledge, relinquishment of its fruit alone is called relinquishment of action, not relinquishment of action in its own form. Thus the Śruti says, ‘doing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years.’ After that, cessation of all action occurs of itself. Thus it is said in the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi: ‘The inward inclination of the intellect, having produced actions from purification, when their purpose is accomplished they disappear, like clouds at the end of the rainy season.’ And the Blessed Lord has said, ‘But the person whose delight is in the Self alone, who is satisfied in the Self and content in the Self alone—for him there is no duty.’ And Vasiṣṭha has said, ‘The yogin should not abandon actions; rather, actions abandon him, through the destruction of resolve itself, which is the root of action.’ Or, seeing that action distracts from steadfastness in knowledge, he may abandon it. Thus the Blessed Lord has said in the Bhāgavata: ‘One should perform actions only so long as one has not become detached, or so long as faith has not arisen in hearing My narrations and so forth. One steadfast in knowledge, detached, or My devotee who is without expectation, having abandoned the āśramas together with their marks, should move beyond the sphere of injunction.’ Enough with excessive elaboration. We return to the matter at hand.

3.translation: For one who does not know, the meaning of the word ‘relinquishment’ is relinquishment of fruit alone, not abandonment of action. To establish precisely this by rejecting another opinion, he presents the difference of views with ‘to be abandoned.’ Some Sāṅkhyas, the thinkers, say that all action is to be abandoned because, having faults such as violence, it binds. Their intention is this: the prohibition ‘one should not injure any beings’ says that violence is a cause of harm to a person. But a contextual injunction such as ‘one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma’ says that violence is an aid to the sacrifice. Therefore, because the two have different objects and do not fall under the relation of general and particular rule, there is no relation of being overridden and overriding. And because violence and the like are possible in all actions accomplished by material things, all action is indeed to be abandoned. Thus it is said: ‘Like what is seen, the scripturally heard means is joined with impurity, decay, and inequality.’ The meaning is: a means such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, although scripturally heard from the teacher’s recitation like a visible means, is taught by revelation, the Veda. In it impurity is violence; through that there is decay, destruction. And among heavens produced by Agnihotra, Jyotiṣṭoma, and so forth there is gradation; another’s superiority makes everyone miserable. But other Mīmāṃsakas say that action such as sacrifice is not to be abandoned. Their intention is this: even though this violence serves the sacrifice, it must be performed by the person; and even when done for another purpose, it is a cause of demerit for the person. For an injunction enjoins performance of what is enjoined for that purpose, since subordination is characterized by being for that purpose. A prohibition, however, does not similarly require that the prohibited act be done for the purpose of the prohibition; it requires only occurrence. Otherwise there would follow absence of fault in violence done through ignorance, carelessness, and so forth. Thus, because injunction and prohibition concern the same object, the general rule is overridden by the particular; therefore there is no fault in the sacrifice, and obligatory sacrificial action is not to be abandoned. By this, equal force of injunction and prohibition is denied, in order to establish the rule of general and particular.

4.translation: Having thus presented the difference of opinions, to state his own view he says ‘decision.’ In this matter of relinquishment, thus disputed, hear the decision from My statement. Do not think, ‘Since relinquishment is well known in the world, what is there to hear here?’ Therefore he says: O tiger among men, O best of men, this relinquishment is difficult to understand. For this abandonment of action is correctly declared by knowers of truth, through discrimination, as threefold by the distinctions beginning with tamasic. He will state its threefoldness beginning with ‘but renunciation of prescribed action.’

6.translation: Showing the manner in which these, when done, become purifying, he says ‘these.’ Those actions beginning with sacrifice which I called purifying—these very actions are to be done. How? Having abandoned attachment, the insistence ‘I am the doer,’ they are to be done solely as worship of the Lord; and having abandoned the fruits, they are to be done. This is My settled view. Therefore it is highest.

7.translation: He now shows the promised threefoldness of relinquishment with the three verses beginning ‘of the prescribed.’ Since desire-motivated action binds, renunciation of it is proper. But renunciation, abandonment, of prescribed obligatory action is not proper, because through purity of sattva it is a cause of liberation. Therefore abandonment of it, characterized by thinking ‘even what is to be adopted is to be abandoned,’ can arise only from delusion. And because delusion is tamasic, that is declared tamasic.

because through purity of sattva it is a cause of liberation
ataḥ tasya parityāgaḥ upādeye api tyājyam iti evaṃ-lakṣaṇāt mohāt eva bhavet
therefore abandonment of it, characterized by thinking ‘even what is to be adopted is to be abandoned,’ can arise only from delusion
sa ca mohasya tāmasatvāt tāmasaḥ parikīrtitaḥ
and because delusion is tamasic, that is declared tamasic

8.translation: He states rajasic relinquishment with ‘painful.’ Without knowledge of the Self as non-doer, merely knowing ‘it is painful,’ if one abandons obligatory action from fear of bodily exertion, such relinquishment is rajasic, because pain belongs to rajas. Therefore, having made that rajasic relinquishment, a rajasic person does not at all obtain the fruit of relinquishment, characterized by steadfastness in knowledge. This is the meaning.
word_for_word: rājasaṃ tyāgam āha — duḥkham iti
he states rajasic relinquishment with ‘painful’
akartṛ-ātma-bodhaṃ vinā kevalaṃ duḥkham iti evaṃ jñātvā
without knowledge of the Self as non-doer, merely knowing ‘it is painful’
śarīra-āyāsa-bhayāt nityaṃ karma tyajet iti yat tādṛśaḥ tyāgo rājasaḥ
if one abandons obligatory action from fear of bodily exertion, such relinquishment is rajasic
duḥkhasya rājasatvāt
because pain belongs to rajas
ataḥ taṃ rājasaṃ tyāgaṃ kṛtvā rājasaḥ puruṣaḥ
therefore, having made that rajasic relinquishment, a rajasic person
tyāgasya phalaṃ jñāna-niṣṭhā-lakṣaṇaṃ na eva labhate
does not at all obtain the fruit of relinquishment, characterized by steadfastness in knowledge
iti arthaḥ
this is the meaning

9.translation: He states sattvic relinquishment with ‘to be done.’ When prescribed action, enjoined as necessarily to be done, is performed after understanding simply ‘it is to be done,’ abandoning attachment and fruit, such relinquishment is considered sattvic.
word_for_word: sāttvikaṃ tyāgam āha — kāryam iti
he states sattvic relinquishment with ‘to be done’
kāryam iti evaṃ buddhvā
after understanding simply ‘it is to be done’
niyatam avaśya-kartavyatayā vihitaṃ karma
prescribed action enjoined as necessarily to be done
saṅgaṃ phalaṃ ca tyaktvā kriyate iti yat
when it is performed abandoning attachment and fruit
tādṛśaḥ tyāgaḥ sāttviko mataḥ
such relinquishment is considered sattvic

10.translation: He states the mark of one established in such sattvic relinquishment with ‘he does not hate.’ Filled with sattva, pervaded by sattva, the sattvic relinquisher does not hate unpleasant, pain-producing action such as bathing early in winter; and he does not cling with affection to pleasant, pleasure-producing action such as midday bathing in the hot season. The reason is: he is intelligent, of steady understanding. He reflects: where even great pain such as humiliation by others is endured and happiness such as heaven is abandoned, how much are these momentary pleasure and pain? Therefore his doubt—false knowledge characterized by the desire to take up bodily pleasure and avoid bodily pain—is cut off.
word_for_word: evaṃ-bhūta-sāttvika-tyāga-pariniṣṭhitasya lakṣaṇam āha — na dveṣṭi iti
he states the mark of one established in such sattvic relinquishment with ‘he does not hate’
sattva-samāviṣṭaḥ sattvena saṃvyāptaḥ sāttvika-tyāgī
filled with sattva, pervaded by sattva, the sattvic relinquisher
akuśalaṃ duḥkha-āvahaṃ śiśire prātaḥ-snāna-ādikaṃ karma na dveṣṭi
does not hate unpleasant, pain-producing action such as bathing early in winter
kuśale ca sukha-kare karmaṇi nidāghe madhyāhna-snāna-ādau na anuṣajjate prītiṃ na karoti
and does not cling with affection to pleasant, pleasure-producing action such as midday bathing in the hot season
tatra hetuḥ medhāvī sthira-buddhiḥ
the reason is: he is intelligent, of steady understanding
yatra para-paribhava-ādi mahat api duḥkhaṃ sahyate svarga-ādi-sukhaṃ ca tyajyate
where even great pain such as humiliation by others is endured and happiness such as heaven is abandoned
tatra kiyat etat tātkālikaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ ca iti evam anusandhānavān
he reflects: how much are these momentary pleasure and pain?
ata eva chinnaḥ saṃśayaḥ mithyā-jñānaṃ daihika-sukha-duḥkhayoḥ upāditsā-parijihīrṣā-lakṣaṇaṃ yasya saḥ
therefore his doubt—false knowledge characterized by desire to take up bodily pleasure and avoid bodily pain—is cut off

11.translation: Objection: rather than such relinquishment of the fruit of action, abandonment of all action would be better; then, because there would be no distraction by action, steadfastness in knowledge would arise easily. To this he says ‘not.’ By an embodied person, one who identifies the body as the Self, it is not possible to abandon all actions without remainder. Thus it has been said, ‘for no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action.’ Therefore, the one who, while performing actions, is a relinquisher of the fruit of action—that one alone is called the principal relinquisher.
word_for_word: nanu evaṃ-bhūtāt karma-phala-tyāgāt varaṃ sarva-karma-tyāgaḥ
objection: rather than such relinquishment of the fruit of action, abandonment of all action would be better
tathā sati karma-vikṣepa-abhāvena jñāna-niṣṭhā sukhaṃ saṃpadyate
then, because there would be no distraction by action, steadfastness in knowledge would arise easily
tatra āha — na iti
to this he says ‘not’
deha-bhṛtā deha-ātma-abhimānavatā niḥśeṣeṇa sarvāṇi karmāṇi tyaktuṃ na hi śakyam
by an embodied person, one who identifies the body as the Self, it is not possible to abandon all actions without remainder
tad uktam — na hi kaścit kṣaṇam api jātu tiṣṭhati akarma-kṛt ity-ādinā
thus it has been said, ‘for no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action’
tasmāt yaḥ tu karmāṇi kurvan eva karma-phala-tyāgī
therefore the one who, while performing actions, is a relinquisher of the fruit of action
sa eva mukhya-tyāgī iti abhidhīyate
that one alone is called the principal relinquisher

12.translation: He states the fruit of such relinquishment of the fruit of action with ‘undesired.’ Undesired means hellish existence; desired means divinity; mixed means humanity. Thus the well-known threefold fruit of sinful action, meritorious action, and action mixed of both arises after death, in the next world, only for non-relinquishers who act with desire, because those three kinds of action arise for them. But it never arises for renouncers. Here, by the word ‘renouncers,’ because of similarity in relinquishment of fruit, the present relinquishers of the fruit of action are also included. For in passages such as ‘he who performs the action that is to be done without depending on its fruit is a renouncer and a yogin,’ the word ‘renouncer’ is seen applied to relinquishers of the fruit of action. For those sattvic persons, because sin does not arise, and because the meritorious fruit has been relinquished by offering it to the Lord, none of the three kinds of fruit of action arises. This is the meaning.
word_for_word: evaṃ-bhūtasya karma-phala-tyāgasya phalam āha — aniṣṭam iti
he states the fruit of such relinquishment of the fruit of action with ‘undesired’
aniṣṭaṃ nārakitvam
undesired means hellish existence
iṣṭaṃ devatvam
desired means divinity
miśraṃ manuṣyatvam
mixed means humanity
evaṃ trividhaṃ pāpasya puṇyasya ca ubhaya-miśrasya ca karmaṇaḥ yat phalaṃ prasiddham
thus the well-known threefold fruit of sinful action, meritorious action, and action mixed of both
tat sarvam atyāgināṃ sakāmānām eva pretya paratra bhavati
all of it arises after death, in the next world, only for non-relinquishers who act with desire
teṣāṃ trividha-karma-saṃbhavāt
because those three kinds of action arise for them
na tu saṃnyāsināṃ kvacid api bhavati
but it never arises for renouncers
saṃnyāsi-śabdena atra phala-tyāga-sāmyāt prakṛtāḥ karma-phala-tyāginaḥ api gṛhyante
here, by the word ‘renouncers,’ because of similarity in relinquishment of fruit, the present relinquishers of the fruit of action are also included
anāśritaḥ karma-phalaṃ kāryaṃ karma karoti yaḥ sa saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca ity-evam-ādau
in passages such as ‘he who performs the action that is to be done without depending on its fruit is a renouncer and a yogin’
karma-phala-tyāgiṣu saṃnyāsi-śabda-prayoga-darśanāt
because the word ‘renouncer’ is seen applied to relinquishers of the fruit of action
teṣāṃ sāttvikānāṃ pāpa-asaṃbhavāt
for those sattvic persons, because sin does not arise
īśvara-arpaṇena ca puṇya-phalasya tyaktatvāt
and because the meritorious fruit has been relinquished by offering it to the Lord
trividham api karma-phalaṃ na bhavati
none of the three kinds of fruit of action arises
iti arthaḥ
this is the meaning

13.translation: Objection: how could the fruit of action not arise for one performing action? Anticipating this, to establish that one who has relinquished attachment and is without ego is not smeared by the fruit of action, he says ‘these five’ in five verses. For the accomplishment, the completion, of all actions, know from My statement these five causes that are about to be stated. To remove the Self’s conceit of doership, these must necessarily be known; praising them for this reason, he says ‘in Sāṅkhya.’ That by which the Supreme Self is correctly declared, known, is Sāṅkhya, knowledge of truth; kṛtānta is that in which the end, completion, of action done in it lies: the settled conclusion of Vedānta. Or, that in which principles are enumerated is Sāṅkhya; that in which an end, a determination, has been made is kṛtānta: the Sāṅkhya scripture itself. They are stated in it; therefore understand them correctly. This is the meaning.
word_for_word: nanu karma kurvataḥ karma-phalaṃ kathaṃ na bhavet iti āśaṅkya
objection: how could the fruit of action not arise for one performing action?
saṅga-tyāginaḥ nirahaṅkārasya sataḥ karma-phalena lepo na asti iti upapādayitum āha — pañca etāni iti pañcabhiḥ
anticipating this, to establish that one who has relinquished attachment and is without ego is not smeared by the fruit of action, he says ‘these five’ in five verses
sarva-karmaṇāṃ siddhaye niṣpattaye
for the accomplishment, the completion, of all actions
imāni vakṣyamāṇāni pañca kāraṇāni me vacanāt nibodha jānīhi
know from My statement these five causes that are about to be stated
ātmanaḥ kartṛtva-abhimāna-nivṛtti-artham avaśyam etāni jñātavyāni
to remove the Self’s conceit of doership, these must necessarily be known
iti evaṃ teṣāṃ stuti-artham āha — sāṃkhye iti
praising them for this reason, he says ‘in Sāṅkhya’
samyak khyāyate jñāyate paramātmā anena iti sāṃkhyaṃ tattva-jñānam
that by which the Supreme Self is correctly declared, known, is Sāṅkhya, knowledge of truth
tasmin kṛtaṃ karma tasya antaḥ samāptiḥ asmin iti kṛtāntaḥ
kṛtānta is that in which the end, completion, of action done in it lies
tasmin vedānta-siddhānte iti arthaḥ
in the settled conclusion of Vedānta: this is the meaning
yad vā saṃkhyāyante gaṇyante tattvāni yasmin iti sāṃkhyam
or, that in which principles are enumerated is Sāṅkhya
kṛtaḥ antaḥ nirṇayo yasmin iti kṛtāntam
that in which an end, a determination, has been made is kṛtānta
sāṃkhya-śāstram eva tasmin proktāni
the Sāṅkhya scripture itself; they are stated in it
ataḥ samyak nibodha iti arthaḥ
therefore understand them correctly: this is the meaning

14.translation: He states those very five with ‘the seat.’ The seat is the body. The doer is ego, the knot of consciousness and the inert. The various instruments are of many kinds, such as the eye and ear. The various activities, distinct in function and in form, are the operations of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth. Here, among these, the fifth cause is the divine factor: Āditya and the other deities that favor the eye and other instruments, or the inner ruler who impels all.
word_for_word: tāni eva āha — adhiṣṭhānam iti
he states those very five with ‘the seat’
adhiṣṭhānaṃ śarīram
the seat is the body
kartā cit-jaḍa-granthiḥ ahaṅkāraḥ
the doer is ego, the knot of consciousness and the inert
pṛthag-vidham aneka-prakāraṃ karaṇaṃ cakṣuḥ-śrotra-ādi
the various instruments are of many kinds, such as the eye and ear
vividhāḥ ca kāryataḥ svarūpataḥ ca pṛthag-bhūtāḥ ceṣṭāḥ prāṇa-apāna-ādīnāṃ vyāpārāḥ
the various activities, distinct in function and in form, are the operations of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth
atra ca eteṣu eva pañcamaṃ daivaṃ ca kāraṇam
here, among these, the fifth cause is the divine factor
cakṣur-ādi-anugrāhakam āditya-ādi
Āditya and the other deities that favor the eye and other instruments
sarva-prerakaḥ antaryāmī vā
or the inner ruler who impels all

15.translation: He states that these alone are the causes of every action with ‘body.’ Action begun by the aforesaid five is included within the three, body, speech, and mind, because threefold action—bodily, verbal, and mental—is well known. Whatever action, righteous or unrighteous, a person performs by body and the others, these five are the causes of all that action.
word_for_word: eteṣām eva sarva-karma-hetutvam āha — śarīra iti
he states that these alone are the causes of every action with ‘body’
yathoktaiḥ pañcabhiḥ prārabhyamāṇaṃ karma triṣu eva antarbhāvya śarīra-vāk-manobhiḥ iti uktam
action begun by the aforesaid five is included within the three, body, speech, and mind
śārīraṃ vācikaṃ mānasaṃ ca trividhaṃ karma iti prasiddheḥ
because threefold action—bodily, verbal, and mental—is well known
śarīra-ādibhiḥ yat yat karma dharmyaṃ vā adharmyaṃ vā karoti naraḥ
whatever action, righteous or unrighteous, a person performs by body and the others
tasya sarvasya karmaṇaḥ ete pañca hetavaḥ
these five are the causes of all that action

16.translation: Then what follows from this? He says ‘there.’ When, in every action, these five are the causes, the person of bad understanding who nevertheless sees the pure, unconditioned, unattached Self alone as the doer, because his intellect has not been refined through the teaching of scripture and teacher, does not see correctly.
word_for_word: tataḥ kim ata āha — tatra iti
then what follows from this? he says ‘there’
tatra sarvasmin karmaṇi ete pañca hetava iti evaṃ sati
when, in every action, these five are the causes
kevalaṃ nirupādhikam asaṅgam ātmānaṃ tu yaḥ kartāraṃ paśyati
the person who nevertheless sees the pure, unconditioned, unattached Self alone as the doer
śāstra-ācārya-upadeśa-tyāgena asaṃskṛta-buddhitvāt durmatiḥ asau
because his intellect has not been refined through the teaching of scripture and teacher, he is of bad understanding
samyak na paśyati
he does not see correctly

17.translation: Who then is of good understanding, for whom the stain of action does not exist as stated? In answer he says ‘whose.’ One in whom there is no intention, ‘I—how am I the doer?’ Or, one in whom the condition of ego, the insistence on doership, does not exist. The meaning is: because he considers the body and the others alone to be the agents of action. Therefore, one whose intellect is not smeared, who does not attach himself to actions through judgments of desired and undesired, such a seer of the Self as distinct from body and the rest, even after killing all these creatures from the standpoint of the world, from his own standpoint, through separateness, does not kill. Nor is he bound by their fruits; he does not obtain bondage. How much less could there be suspicion of bondage for him from actions that, through purity of sattva, cause the arising of indirect knowledge? Thus it is said: ‘he who performs actions, placing them in Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not smeared by sin.’
word_for_word: kaḥ tarhi sumatiḥ yasya karma-lepo na asti iti uktam iti apekṣāyām āha — yasya iti
who then is of good understanding, for whom the stain of action does not exist as stated? in answer he says ‘whose’
aham iti kutaḥ ahaṃ kartā iti evaṃ-bhūto bhāvaḥ abhiprāyaḥ yasya na asti
one in whom there is no intention, ‘I—how am I the doer?’
yad vā ahaṃ-kṛtaḥ ahaṅkārasya bhāvaḥ kartṛtva-abhiniveśo yasya na asti
or one in whom the condition of ego, the insistence on doership, does not exist
śarīra-ādīnām eva karma-kartṛtva-ālocanāt iti arthaḥ
because he considers the body and the others alone to be the agents of action: this is the meaning
ata eva yasya buddhiḥ na lipyate iṣṭa-aniṣṭa-buddhyā karmasu na sajjate
therefore, one whose intellect is not smeared, who does not attach himself to actions through judgments of desired and undesired
sa evaṃ-bhūto deha-ādi-vyatirikta-ātma-darśī
such a seer of the Self as distinct from body and the rest
imān lokān sarvān api prāṇinaḥ loka-dṛṣṭyā hatvā api
even after killing all these creatures from the standpoint of the world
viviktatayā sva-dṛṣṭyā na hanti
from his own standpoint, through separateness, he does not kill
na ca tat-phalaiḥ nibadhyate bandhanaṃ na prāpnoti
nor is he bound by their fruits; he does not obtain bondage
kiṃ punaḥ sattva-śuddhi-dvārā parokṣa-jñāna-utpatti-hetubhiḥ karmabhiḥ tasya bandha-śaṅkā iti arthaḥ
how much less could there be suspicion of bondage for him from actions that, through purity of sattva, cause the arising of indirect knowledge? this is the meaning
tad uktam brahmaṇi ādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ lipyate na sa pāpena iti
thus it is said: ‘he who performs actions, placing them in Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not smeared by sin’

18.translation: To establish precisely that, ‘even after killing, he does not kill and is not bound,’ with the intention that, since the prompting of action, the basis of action, the fruits of action, and so forth are composed of the three guṇas, the guṇa-less Self has no relation to them, he states the prompting of action and the basis of action with ‘knowledge.’ Knowledge is the cognition, ‘this is a means to what is desired.’ The knowable is the action that is a means to what is desired. The knower is the locus of such knowledge. Thus the prompting of action is threefold. That by which one is impelled, set in motion, is prompting; the triad beginning with knowledge is the cause of engagement in action. Or ‘prompting’ means injunction. Thus the Bhaṭṭas have said: ‘prompting, instruction, and injunction are words with one meaning.’ Then the meaning is: relying on the triad beginning with knowledge, of the stated character and composed of the three guṇas, the injunction to action operates. Thus it is said: ‘the Vedas have the three guṇas as their sphere.’ Likewise, an instrument is the most effective means; action is what the doer most wishes to attain; the doer is the producer of the activity. That in which action is gathered is the aggregate of action. Thus the threefold causal factor beginning with instrument is the direct basis of activity. The other three causal factors, beginning with recipient, produce the activity only indirectly, not as its direct basis. Therefore only the triad beginning with instrument is called the basis of activity.
word_for_word: hatvā api na hanti na nibadhyate iti etad eva upapādayitum
to establish precisely that ‘even after killing, he does not kill and is not bound’
karma-codanāyāḥ karma-āśrayasya ca karma-phala-ādīnāṃ ca triguṇa-ātmakatvāt
since the prompting of action, the basis of action, the fruits of action, and so forth are composed of the three guṇas
nirguṇasya ātmanaḥ tat-saṃbandho na asti iti abhiprāyeṇa
with the intention that the guṇa-less Self has no relation to them
karma-codanāṃ karma-āśrayaṃ ca āha — jñānam iti
he states the prompting of action and the basis of action with ‘knowledge’
jñānam iṣṭa-sādhanam etad iti bodhaḥ
knowledge is the cognition ‘this is a means to what is desired’
jñeyam iṣṭa-sādhanaṃ karma
the knowable is the action that is a means to what is desired
parijñātā evaṃ-bhūta-jñāna-āśrayaḥ
the knower is the locus of such knowledge
evaṃ trividhā karma-codanā
thus the prompting of action is threefold
codyate pravartyate yena iti codanā
that by which one is impelled, set in motion, is prompting
jñāna-ādi-tritayaṃ karma-pravṛtti-hetuḥ iti arthaḥ
the triad beginning with knowledge is the cause of engagement in action: this is the meaning
yad vā codanā iti vidhiḥ ucyate
or ‘prompting’ means injunction
tad uktaṃ bhaṭṭaiḥ codanā ca upadeśaḥ ca vidhiḥ ca eka-artha-vācinaḥ iti
thus the Bhaṭṭas have said: ‘prompting, instruction, and injunction are words with one meaning’
tataḥ ca ayam arthaḥ
then the meaning is
ukta-lakṣaṇaṃ triguṇa-ātmakaṃ jñāna-ādi-trayam avalambya karma-vidhiḥ pravartate iti
relying on the triad beginning with knowledge, of the stated character and composed of the three guṇas, the injunction to action operates
tad uktam traiguṇya-viṣayā vedāḥ iti
thus it is said: ‘the Vedas have the three guṇas as their sphere’
tathā ca karaṇaṃ sādhakatamam
likewise, an instrument is the most effective means
karma ca kartuḥ īpsitatamam
action is what the doer most wishes to attain
kartā kriyā-nirvartakaḥ
the doer is the producer of the activity
karma saṃgṛhyate asmin iti karma-saṃgrahaḥ
that in which action is gathered is the aggregate of action
karaṇa-ādi-trividhaṃ kārakaṃ kriyā-āśraya iti arthaḥ
the threefold causal factor beginning with instrument is the direct basis of activity: this is the meaning
saṃpradāna-ādi-kāraka-trayaṃ tu paraṃparayā kriyā-nirvartakam eva kevalaṃ
the other three causal factors, beginning with recipient, produce the activity only indirectly
na tu sākṣāt kriyāyā āśrayaḥ
not as its direct basis
ataḥ karaṇa-ādi-tritayam eva kriyā-āśraya iti uktam
therefore only the triad beginning with instrument is called the basis of activity

19.translation: Then what follows? He says ‘knowledge.’ That in which the guṇas are correctly described according to differences of effects is ‘enumeration of the guṇas,’ the Sāṅkhya scripture. In it, knowledge, action, and the doer are each spoken of as threefold according to the distinctions of sattva and the other guṇas. Hear also those forthcoming kinds of knowledge and so forth exactly as they are. The restrictive ‘threefold indeed’ serves to deny intrinsic doership and the like to the Self apart from the limiting adjuncts of the three guṇas. In the fourteenth chapter, beginning with ‘there sattva, because of its purity,’ the manner in which the guṇas bind was explained. In the seventeenth chapter, beginning with ‘the sattvic worship the gods,’ by explaining the threefold nature made by the guṇas, it was said that the nature of rajas and tamas should be abandoned and a sattvic nature produced through use of sattvic food and so forth. Here, however, to show that action, causal factors, fruits, and so forth have no relation to the Self, all of them are said to be composed of the three guṇas. This distinction is to be understood.
word_for_word: tataḥ kim ata āha — jñānam iti
then what follows? he says ‘knowledge’
guṇāḥ samyak kārya-bhedena khyāyante pratipādyante asmin iti guṇa-saṃkhyānaṃ sāṃkhya-śāstram
that in which the guṇas are correctly described according to differences of effects is ‘enumeration of the guṇas,’ the Sāṅkhya scripture
tasmin jñānaṃ karma ca kriyā kartā ca pratyekaṃ sattva-ādi-guṇa-bhedena tridhā eva ucyate
in it, knowledge, action, and the doer are each spoken of as threefold according to the distinctions of sattva and the other guṇas
tāni api jñāna-ādīni vakṣyamāṇāni yathāvat śṛṇu
hear also those forthcoming kinds of knowledge and so forth exactly as they are
tridhā eva iti eva-kāraḥ guṇa-traya-upādhi-vyatirekeṇa ātmanaḥ svataḥ kartṛtva-ādi-pratiṣedha-arthaḥ
the restrictive ‘threefold indeed’ serves to deny intrinsic doership and the like to the Self apart from the limiting adjuncts of the three guṇas
caturdaśe adhyāye tatra sattvaṃ nirmalatvāt ity-ādinā guṇānāṃ bandhakatva-prakāro nirūpitaḥ
in the fourteenth chapter, beginning with ‘there sattva, because of its purity,’ the manner in which the guṇas bind was explained
saptadaśe adhyāye yajante sāttvikā devān ity-ādinā guṇa-kṛta-trividha-svabhāva-nirūpaṇena
in the seventeenth chapter, beginning with ‘the sattvic worship the gods,’ by explaining the threefold nature made by the guṇas
rajas-tamaḥ-svabhāvaṃ parityajya sāttvika-āhāra-ādi-sevayā sāttvika-svabhāvaḥ saṃpādanīya iti uktam
it was said that the nature of rajas and tamas should be abandoned and a sattvic nature produced through use of sattvic food and so forth
iha tu kriyā-kāraka-phala-ādīnām ātma-saṃbandho na asti iti darśayitum
here, however, to show that action, causal factors, fruits, and so forth have no relation to the Self
sarveṣāṃ triguṇa-ātmakatvam ucyate iti viśeṣo jñātavyaḥ
all of them are said to be composed of the three guṇas; this distinction is to be understood

20.translation: There, he states the threefoldness of knowledge, beginning with sattvic, in the three verses beginning ‘in all beings.’ In all beings, from Brahmā down to immovable things, which are divided and mutually distinct, the knowledge by which one sees, contemplates, one undivided, continuous, imperishable, changeless reality—the truth of the Supreme Self—that knowledge you should know as sattvic.
word_for_word: tatra jñānasya sāttvika-ādi-traividhyam āha — sarva-bhūteṣu iti tribhiḥ
there, he states the threefoldness of knowledge, beginning with sattvic, in the three verses beginning ‘in all beings’
sarveṣu bhūteṣu brahmādi-sthāvara-anteṣu vibhakteṣu parasparaṃ vyāvṛtteṣu
in all beings, from Brahmā down to immovable things, which are divided and mutually distinct
avibhaktam anusyūtaṃ ekam avyayaṃ nirvikāraṃ bhāvaṃ paramātma-tattvam
one undivided, continuous, imperishable, changeless reality—the truth of the Supreme Self
yena jñānena īkṣate ālocayati
the knowledge by which one sees, contemplates
tat jñānaṃ sāttvikaṃ viddhi
that knowledge you should know as sattvic
